edits.text:
At a coprime degree-n target the linear monic interpolation system for the
2n+1 coefficient coordinates is invertible. For a null variation dP,dQ, with
degree(dP)<=n and degree(dQ)<=n-1, the cross polynomial dP*Q-P*dQ has degree
at most 2n. Vanishing at 2n+1 distinct points makes it identically zero.
Coprimality then gives (dP,dQ)=(cP,cQ), and the monic-denominator variation
forces c=0. Thus local coefficient recovery from the sample vector is smooth
and rational wherever that interpolation determinant is nonzero.

Delete loops and components not connected to a port; disconnected ports are
an open circuit. For a connected LC port graph, each term of the spanning-tree
denominator contains n-1 admittance factors; each term of the two-forest
numerator contains n-2. Each LC admittance is either C*s or 1/(L*s).
Multiplying both by s^(number of L) yields nonnegative-coefficient polynomials
of degree at most the total reactive count, with opposite parity. This follows
from term parity n-1 and n-2 before the common multiplication; zero terms do
not alter it. Do not assume a nonzero constant coefficient: both polynomials
can have a common power of s. Shorted ports give Gamma=-1.

edits.text: Assume for contradiction E<=delta=\(10^{-150}\). The inherited all-three-reactive margin is strictly \(10^{-13}\). Put \(\eta=2\cdot10^{-14}=1/50000000000000\). An L or C outside [eta,1/eta] can be deleted or contracted, reducing the useful reactive count to at most three with uniform positive-real reflection change <=4*eta. For small L, contract and use 2*s*L; for large L, open and use 2/(s*L). For small C, open and use 2*s*C; for large C, contract and use 2/(s*C). These are the inherited positive-real branch surgery estimates, valid at the seven samples even when deletion or contraction changes connectivity. If the resulting port is open or short, compare Gamma=1 or -1 directly; their errors are at least mu. Apply the inherited three-reactive theorem only to the remaining finite positive port graphs with distinct terminals. Since delta+4*eta<\(10^{-13}\), the result would contradict the inherited margin. Consequently every useful L/C lies in the stated box; redundant loops or detached components must first be removed, and if fewer than four useful reactive edges remain the inherited margin applies immediately.

edits.text:
Endpoint-lemma proof: drive the port at unit voltage.
For each real s>0, the effective conductance is the minimum of
 sum_L (v_u-v_v)^2/(s*L) + sum_R (v_u-v_v)^2/R
     + sum_C s*C*(v_u-v_v)^2
over port-fixed potentials. Clipping to [0,1] never increases the energy, so
the admissible set is compact. If an L-only path joins the ports, its series
impedance tends to zero and Rayleigh comparison forces Z->0. Otherwise,
there are admissible potentials constant on every L-connected component.
On that constraint set, minimize the sole-resistor energy and call the value
Y0. Testing with a minimizer gives limsup Y(s)<=Y0 because its capacitor
energy vanishes. Along any minimizing sequence with bounded energy, every
L drop tends to zero. Compactness yields a subsequential limit in the
constraint set; nonnegativity of all omitted energies then gives
liminf Y(s)>=Y0. Thus Y(s)->Y0. After L contraction and C deletion, a graph
with one resistor has positive conductance only if that resistor connects
the two distinct port components, in which case Y0=1/R. If Y0=0, the port
impedance tends to infinity. Replacing s by 1/t exchanges the roles of L
and C for the infinity limit. This proof also covers R loops and detached
components, without assuming a nonsingular imaginary-frequency matrix.

figures.alt: Load rotation on the Smith chart
figures.description: The marked load is converted from impedance to a point inside the reflection disk. Its transmission-line trajectory follows a circle of constant reflection magnitude. The direction and angle describe propagation toward the source. This geometric rotation is separate from the cyclic coefficient projectors introduced in the packet calculations.

figures.alt: Order-three impedance and admittance packets
figures.description: Two groups of three bars show the order-three packet contributions to the impedance coordinate and to its reciprocal admittance. Adding every contribution in a group reconstructs that function. The admittance contributions are calculated from the reciprocal function; they are not obtained by taking the reciprocal of each impedance packet. The adjacent worked example gives the exact values.

figures.alt: Packet truncation can violate passivity
figures.description: The complete passive response is compared with the sum after a packet is discarded. The truncated response crosses the unit-reflection bound. A value outside that bound corresponds to a negative real part of normalized impedance. The example demonstrates why a bound on the complete response cannot be assumed for an arbitrary truncated representation.

figures.alt: Individually safe packet selections can have an unsafe union
figures.description: The packet bars and retained sums compare two residue-coset selections with their union. Each individual selection is contractive for every Schur response under the stated coset rule. The union recreates a sum that exceeds the passive bound in the exact example. The safe-selection property therefore requires a condition on the complete mask.

figures.alt: Signed hard-mask weights and nonnegative Fejér weights
figures.description: The hard packet mask has a negative weight when expressed as an average of cyclic rotations. The Fejér replacement has nonnegative weights summing to one. The adjacent theorem identifies the sum of absolute rotation weights as the universal filter norm and quantifies the least possible repair distance for the displayed signed mask.

figures.alt: A hard filter leaves the passive disk while the Fejér filter stays inside
figures.description: The main Smith-disk comparison marks the original response, the hard-filtered response, and the Fejér-filtered response. The hard-filtered value lies outside the unit circle in the exact example. The inset follows the same responses as the real load variable changes. The universal Fejér guarantee follows from its nonnegative rotation weights; the plot illustrates that theorem.

figures.alt: Eigenvalue certificates for two matrix-interpolation datasets
figures.description: The feasible noncommuting dataset has four positive Pick-matrix eigenvalues. The incompatible dataset has negative eigenvalues even though its measured node matrices are individually contractive. The comparison illustrates the difference between checking each observation and checking joint interpolation compatibility. Exact minors and a negative quadratic-form witness are supplied in the surrounding text.

figures.alt: Curved feasible region for two real packets
figures.description: The horizontal axis is the real even packet p zero; the vertical axis is the real odd packet p one. The symmetric feasible region has horizontal tips at plus or minus one with p one zero, and vertical tips at plus or minus one half with p zero zero. Retaining a vertical-tip value exactly forces the other packet to zero. A horizontal displacement from that tip is infeasible. The neighboring formula gives the complete curved boundary.

figures.alt: Pairwise frequency compatibility does not imply joint compatibility
figures.description: Three frequency nodes are connected by edges representing feasible two-frequency interpolation problems. Although every edge passes its pair test, the complete three-node Pick matrix fails positivity. The graph records logical compatibility between observations, rather than physical wires between circuit nodes. The accompanying matrix calculation supplies the joint obstruction.

figures.alt: Separate slices and the joint bidisk condition
figures.description: The parameter diagram compares tests that hold on individual frequency or load slices with the stronger condition for one jointly contractive bidisk response. At the fixed parameter indicated in the caption, a slice-admissible region extends beyond the joint threshold. The example isolates a compatibility constraint that is invisible when the two variables are tested separately.

figures.alt: An odd winding obstructs a holomorphic reciprocal factor
figures.description: The first load coefficient follows a closed contour that winds once around zero. A holomorphic square has even winding around such a contour when the boundary is nonzero. The mismatch rules out the required global square factor for the specified reciprocal model. This is an analytic factorization obstruction, separate from pointwise passivity.

figures.alt: Three-reactive circuit with two series-connected passive blocks
figures.description: The input connects block A, a middle resistor, and block B in series. Block A is a resistor in parallel with an inductor. Block B has a resistor, a series resistor–inductor branch, and a capacitor in parallel. The circuit contains four resistors, two inductors, and one capacitor. The labels give normalized values; the adjoining equations define the exact realization.

figures.alt: Lossless boundary reflection and its dissipative filtered response
figures.description: The Smith-disk panel compares the original ideal-inductor response on the unit circle with the safely filtered response inside it. The frequency panel shows the filtered normalized input resistance becoming positive while the original resistance is zero. Both panels illustrate the same exact rational realization; sampled traces do not supply the identity proof.

figures.alt: Exact degree growth and a canceling pole-pair limit
figures.description: The bar panel compares rational degree before and after safe filtering for the inductor and series-LC examples. The pole panel follows the extra complex-conjugate pair as the automorphism parameter changes. As that parameter approaches zero, the pair approaches a factor that cancels in the limit. Exact degree and effective approximation order therefore answer different questions. The third, real pole is omitted from the trajectory panel for scale.

figures.alt: A proved dissipation envelope and a sampled boundary comparison
figures.description: The horizontal axis is the inductor automorphism parameter. The vertical axis is the boundary dissipation quantity one minus squared reflection magnitude. One curve is an analytically proved lower envelope for every boundary angle; the other is a numerical minimum over sampled angles. The marked one-third example has a separate exact extremum certificate. The sampled curve is supporting context.

figures.alt: Safe filtering of a lossless series-LC response
figures.description: The first panel shows the original lossless reflection on the Smith boundary and the filtered reflection in the passive interior. The second compares their normalized input resistance across angular frequency. The filtered rational response has degree six, and its minimum-six realization is given separately. Physical example values in the diagram refer to an ideal model with the stated reference and time scale.

figures.alt: One-inductor passive approximation and two different error measures
figures.description: The circuit panel has a series resistor followed by a resistor and inductor in parallel. The next panels plot absolute reflection error and normalized impedance error against dimensionless angular frequency. Their sharp bounds are four divided by forty-five for reflection and one for impedance. These different values demonstrate why an approximation must name its error coordinate. The plotted curves come from exact rational formulas.

figures.alt: High exact degree with exponentially decreasing one-inductor approximation error
figures.description: The logarithmic plot shows the sharp uniform reflection error for the positive cyclic-mask examples. Each point has its own exact rational degree, while the same one-inductor RL response approximates the family. The error decreases according to the displayed analytical formula. The comparison separates exact degree from the order required at a chosen approximation tolerance.

figures.alt: Series resistor followed by a parallel resistor–inductor branch
figures.description: Starting at the upper input terminal, pass through the series resistor R sub s to a node shared by R sub p and the inductor L. Those two branches are in parallel and return to the lower input terminal. All three components are positive under the hypotheses in the adjacent first-order theorem.

figures.alt: Certified eight-node circuit with three inductors and three capacitors
figures.description: The port is between node one and ground node zero; nodes two through seven are internal. Resistors connect node pairs zero–three, zero–four, one–five, one–six, two–five, three–six, and four–seven. Inductors connect zero–five, two–three, and three–seven. Capacitors connect zero–six, one–two, and four–five. The adjoining table gives approximate normalized values, and the rational root certificate defines the exact positive values. The reactive minimum is six.
figures.caption: The positive eight-node realization has three inductors, three capacitors, and seven resistors. Its exact root certificate and the degree lower bound establish reactive minimum six.

figures.alt: Two regular balanced cores and a certified perturbation region
figures.description: The forest core has a four-edge active LC path and two resistor links. The cyclic core has an active parallel LC pair, two other reactive branches, and two resistor links. Under the stated exact endpoint, resonance, derivative, and regularity conditions, every allowed balanced response has one of these two forms. A supplied neighborhood permits at most one-percent retained-component error and a combined resistor-surgery budget of one ten-thousandth; its positive-real sample error exceeds one three-hundredth.

figures.alt: A port-zero internal mode and an inversion-symmetric response
figures.description: The representative balanced mode has zero voltage at both port attachments and equal nonzero internal mode levels. Its four reactive branches form a matched structure; the internal resistor network connects equal-level vertices. The classification gives either a response with at most three reactives or frequency-inversion symmetry. The displayed detuning and weak-coupling region has a positive-real error bound greater than three fortieths. A source-free internal mode and a loss-free driven state are distinct hypotheses.

figures.alt: Coefficient constraints, physical energy, and reactive rounding
figures.description: The coefficient diagram removes an unstable part of the admissible polygon, leaving a stable triangle. The accompanying panels state whole-class one-inductor and one-capacitor bounds at reactive budgets three and four, with arbitrary finite resistors. Further panels give the normalized component-range conclusion for a sufficiently close fit. These are structural positive-real constraints; the displayed small constants are not component manufacturing tolerances.

figures.alt: Series-class margins and five resistor-template reductions
figures.description: One panel treats a series inductor followed by an RC body; another treats a series capacitor followed by an RL body. The respective positive-real reflection margins are one over two thousand and one over five hundred thousand. The coefficient panels reduce near-target polynomials to a segment or polygon. Five common resistor templates retain the mixed placements through physical open and wire faces. The global transfer argument supplies an additional physical constraint.

figures.alt: Resistor-backbone scale gaps lead to modes or zero-loss cores
figures.description: Resistor-only elimination retains the terminals and reactive endpoints, giving at most ten vertices and forty-five resistor slots. A spanning forest has at most nine edges, so a scale gap permits controlled opening and contraction. A small natural driven denominator leads to a repaired internal mode; the regular case leads to a repaired zero-loss driven state and a response chart. The conclusion is a topology-uniform, extremely small positive-real separation, with larger bounds under the stated state hypotheses.

figures.alt: Guaranteed reflection uncertainty disks for a damped mixed-RLC example
figures.description: The main panel locates the nominal responses inside the passive reflection disk. The magnified panel shows guaranteed uncertainty disks at angular frequencies one half, one, and two. Independent one-percent variations and the specified series-loss budget are included. At the nominal match, the exact reflected-power bound is below one divided by three hundred eighty-five. The disks are analytic guarantees for the ideal model, rather than a cloud of measured or sampled outcomes.

figures.alt: Sylvester signs force a three-inductor, three-capacitor signature
figures.description: The determinant-sign sequence is positive, negative, negative, positive, positive, positive, negative. It has three changes and three permanences under the stated signature rule. For a realization using exactly six reactive elements, the conclusion is three inductors and three capacitors. The signature constrains component kinds; it does not determine all connections or resistor values.

figures.alt: Real-Laplace impedance and its unique slope crossover
figures.description: The upper panel plots normalized impedance against positive real Laplace argument; both endpoint values are three. The lower panel plots its derivative, which changes sign at the single marked crossover near zero point three three five three one. The adjacent exact argument gives uniqueness. These are real-Laplace response and slope plots, not sinusoidal impedance measurements.

figures.alt: Finite five-node pruning counts
figures.description: The bars show fourteen thousand four hundred labeled placements, three thousand two hundred forty-nine after endpoint-short exclusions, two thousand five hundred after same-type-cycle exclusions, and one thousand nine hundred thirty-four with both slope signs possible. The final row has one hundred sixty-eight terminal-preserving symmetry classes and uses a different counting unit. Passing these filters does not prove that a placement realizes the target.

figures.alt: Rejected and retained reactive placements
figures.description: The left example has every capacitor shorted by an inductive path in the DC limit and fails the stated endpoint condition. The right example retains a possible capacitor voltage and passes this particular rejection rule. Inductors and capacitors are distinguished by their branch symbols as well as color; resistors may connect any node pair. Passing the rule does not establish realizability.

figures.alt: Pole pairs of a two-state section and its complement
figures.description: The complex-frequency plot separates the poles assigned to the extracted two-state section from the remaining conjugate pole pairs. Real and imaginary axes describe pole locations, not physical node positions. The adjoining rational formulas define the decomposition and verify pole allocation; the diagram is an illustration of those exact identities.

figures.alt: Positive-real parts of a target and two complementary sections
figures.description: The frequency curves show the real part of the degree-six target impedance and of the extracted two-state section and its complement. Each complementary response is passive under the stated exact inequalities, and their sum is the target. Positivity is supplied by the accompanying algebraic argument, rather than by the finite plot alone.

figures.alt: Transformer-free two-reactive triangle section
figures.description: The three-node circuit has a resistor directly between input node one and ground node zero. A resistor and inductor are in parallel between nodes one and two. A resistor and capacitor are in parallel between nodes two and zero. The exact normalized values are given in the adjacent component table. The graph realizes the selected real-pole section with two reactive components; the complementary response has its own realization question.
figures.caption: A one-inductor, one-capacitor realization of the real-pole section.

figures.alt: Two realizable pole-pair sections and one two-reactive obstruction
figures.description: The real and lower-complex pole-pair sections each have a one-inductor, one-capacitor realization. The upper section is positive-real but fails the stated two-reactive realizability conditions. Independent two-reactive synthesis of all three sections therefore cannot attain six reactives. The full target has a coupled eight-node minimum-six realization with different interconnections.

figures.alt: Second transformer-free one-inductor, one-capacitor section
figures.description: The three-node circuit has a capacitor and resistor in parallel directly between input node one and ground node zero. Another resistor joins the input to internal node two. A resistor and inductor are in parallel between node two and ground. The neighboring coefficient formulas define the exact positive normalized values for the lower complex pole-pair section.

figures.alt: Regularity tests for the upper pole-pair section
figures.description: The diagram evaluates the classical biquadratic regularity inequalities for the upper-frequency section. The indicated signs fail the relevant two-reactive regularity alternatives over the stated allocation. The argument must also treat the exceptional bridge cases, which are addressed in the following figure and proof.

figures.alt: Exceptional bridge tests across the complete constant-allocation interval
figures.description: The plotted bridge invariants are evaluated over the full physically allowed constant allocation. Their certified signs exclude the applicable exceptional two-reactive bridge alternatives. Together with the regularity inequalities, this establishes the stated pole-pair obstruction. The conclusion concerns this extracted section and reactive budget, rather than all topologies for the complete degree-six target.

figures.alt: Two passive responses with the same finite interpolation anchors
figures.description: Two Smith-disk trajectories pass through the marked anchor values and separate between them. Both responses satisfy their stated passivity conditions. The example demonstrates that agreement at finitely many observations can leave ambiguity in the full response. The complete rational formulas and shared data are given in the surrounding interpolation calculation.

figures.alt: Boundary reflection norms of the target and cubic interpolant
figures.description: The plotted boundary magnitudes compare the degree-six target with the cubic interpolant. Certified bounds accompany the curves, so the passivity conclusions come from exact inequalities. The fact that both curves remain within the passive limit does not make the two rational responses identical.

figures.alt: Frequency-dependent reflection error with an exact shared point
figures.description: The graph plots the absolute reflection difference between the target and its cubic interpolant over frequency. A marked interpolation point has exact agreement, while the responses differ elsewhere. The adjoining bounds quantify that difference and specify the comparison domain.

figures.alt: Passive cubic section with four resistors and three reactives
figures.description: Ground is node zero, the input is node one, and nodes two and three are internal. Resistors connect zero–two, zero–three, one–two, and two–three. Inductors connect zero–three and one–two; the capacitor connects one–three. The graph has four positive resistors, two inductors, and one capacitor. The rational contraction certificate defines exact positive component values and proves the cubic target identity.

figures.alt: Two passive cubic responses sum to the degree-six target
figures.description: The comparison shows the target response and its two complementary cubic sections. The sections are added as impedances, corresponding to series connection of the one-ports. Each has its own passivity argument. The identity of their sum does not imply that both sections have three-reactive ordinary realizations.

figures.alt: Component graphs of a seven-reactive series realization
figures.description: Section A has resistor edges zero–two, zero–three, one–two, and two–three; inductors zero–three and one–two; and a capacitor one–three. Section B has resistors on all ten pairs of five nodes, inductors two–four and zero–three, and capacitors three–four and one–two. Series connection gives seven reactives in total. This is an exact realization with a count distinct from the separate minimum-six construction.

figures.alt: A common pole and zero hide one internal mode at the port
figures.description: The complex-frequency plot marks numerator zeros and denominator poles for the four-reactive section B. One real zero and pole coincide in an exact common factor. Canceling that factor gives a cubic driving-point impedance while the four physical storage elements remain. The cancellation is algebraic and is separately certified.

figures.alt: Seven physical storage elements with degree six at the port
figures.description: The construction diagram series-connects section A, with three reactives, and section B, with four. Each reduced impedance is cubic, so their combined reduced degree is six in the stated exact construction. Section B has one common factor in its natural numerator and denominator. Removing that factor from the response formula does not remove a physical branch.

figures.alt: Six reactive states in a model with an ideal reciprocal combiner
figures.description: The external port connects to a static reciprocal three-port combiner with isolated output ports. One output feeds a degree-two series-LC response and the other a degree-four RLC response. Their reactive counts are two and four. The ideal modal transformer is an additional permitted element in this chapter; the ordinary transformer-free minimum-six circuit is a separate construction.

figures.alt: Four-reactive one-port for the conjugate-rotation response
figures.description: The one-port contains a lossless parallel LC tank followed in series by a resistor in parallel with a series RLC branch. The tank values are L equals forty-eight divided by thirty-five and C equals thirty-five divided by forty-eight. The second block has parallel resistance one, series resistance twenty-five divided by twenty-four, L equals thirty-five divided by forty-eight, and C equals forty-eight divided by thirty-five. All are exact positive normalized values.
figures.caption: A parallel LC tank is in series with a resistor in parallel with a series RLC branch. Every labeled normalized component value is an exact positive rational.

figures.alt: Smith trajectories and the uniform four-fifths reflection bound
figures.description: The Smith-disk panel compares the original lossless response, its conjugate response, and the combined six-state response. The boundary-phase panel plots their reflection magnitudes and the certified four-fifths upper bound for the combined response. The algebraic checker establishes that bound over the entire stated boundary.

figures.alt: Positive polynomial certificate for a reflection bound
figures.description: The horizontal variable is twice the cosine of boundary phase, ranging from minus two to two. The plotted polynomial is sixteen twenty-fifths times the squared-denominator expression minus the squared-numerator expression. Positive rational Bernstein coefficients on the two subintervals certify its positivity. That certificate establishes the four-fifths reflection bound; the plot illustrates the certificate.

figures.alt: Resistor-only node elimination preserves the port response
figures.description: The before-and-after network diagrams show a pure resistor interior node replaced by effective resistor connections among retained nodes. The rational example implements a Laplacian Schur complement and preserves the port impedance. Reactive endpoints are retained; this rule does not replace arbitrary reactive subnetworks by ordinary resistor edges.

figures.alt: A threshold obstruction for a universal resistor-only mixer
figures.description: The diagram separates the admissible region from the region above the proved mixing threshold. The obstruction applies to the specified fixed resistor-only scaffold combining two supplied networks. It does not exclude a differently interconnected RLC realization of the complete target, such as the certified minimum-six graph.
